findings.title: Blocked email match is case-sensitive and unnormalized, so it is trivially bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact string lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email)`) against the raw email entered on the signup form. The rest of the codebase normalizes email via Email.downcase (which lowercases and strips dots/plus tags for gmail-style providers) before storing/comparing, but this lookup does not. A blocked address like bad@spammer.com can be evaded simply by signing up as Bad@Spammer.com, or with gmail dot/plus variants (b.ad+1@gmail.com). Since the entire purpose of the feature is to keep blocked users out, the lookup should normalize the incoming email the same way User emails are normalized, and the blocked_emails rows should be stored normalized.

findings.title: match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: should_block? loads the record, does `record.match_count += 1`, and saves. Under concurrent signups/validations hitting the same blocked email, increments will be lost (last writer wins). Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...")` or update_counters so the statistics are accurate.

findings.title: Blocked check is skipped whenever any other email error exists
findings.body: The BlockedEmail.should_block? call is guarded by `record.errors[attribute].blank?`, and each User.save with a changed email runs this validator. The intent is fine, but note that should_block? has a side effect (incrementing match_count and last_match_at) — because it runs inside model validation, any save of a user whose email changed (including admin edits, seed scripts, etc.) mutates these statistics, while genuinely blocked attempts that also fail format validation are never counted. If the stats are meant to record blocked signup attempts specifically, the counting should happen at the controller/signup path rather than inside a model validator.
